practiceQuestions.q: Who among the following European travellers provided a detailed account of the opulence of the Mughal ruling class alongside the acute poverty of the peasantry in his travelogue 'Travels in the Mogul Empire'?
opts: Sir Thomas Roe
François Bernier
Jean-Baptiste Tavernier
Peter Mundy
practiceQuestions.sol: François Bernier, a French physician and traveller who spent twelve years at the Mughal court, sharply contrasted the extreme luxury of the Mughal nobility with the impoverished conditions of the general populace and peasantry, arguing that the lack of private property in land undermined standard of living. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part II]

practiceQuestions.q: In the context of Mughal administration and social hierarchy, what did the term 'Khalisah' refer to?
opts: Lands held by autonomous hereditary chiefs (Zamindars)
Crown lands whose revenues went directly to the imperial exchequer
Tax-free grants given to religious scholars and institutions
Military cantonments established along the imperial frontiers
practiceQuestions.sol: Khalisah lands were crown lands directly managed by the imperial administration, and their revenues were channeled directly to the emperor's treasury, distinguishing them from Jagir lands assigned to Mansabdars. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History / Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following terms was used in Mughal India to designate revenue-free land grants given for charitable, religious, or educational purposes?
opts: Paibaqi
Madad-i-maash
Peshlash
Tamgha
practiceQuestions.sol: 'Madad-i-maash' (also known as suyurghal) were revenue grants bestowed by the Mughal emperors upon learned men, religious figures, and the destitute to support their livelihood and maintain standard of living. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: The standard of living of the rural masses in Mughal India was largely tied to the village community. What was the term used for the village headman?
opts: Muqaddam or Mandal
Qanungo
Patwari
Amin
practiceQuestions.sol: The village headman was known as the Muqaddam or Mandal. He represented the village in interactions with state officials for revenue collection and maintained local order. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari / NCERT Class 11]

practiceQuestions.q: According to Abul Fazl's 'Ain-i-Akbari', what was the primary source of state revenue that directly impacted the economic well-being and consumption levels of the Indian peasantry?
opts: Maritime trade tariffs
Land revenue (Mal)
Professional taxes on urban artisans
Tribute from tributary rulers
practiceQuestions.sol: Land revenue constituted the backbone of Mughal state finance, absorbing a major share of agricultural produce and heavily dictating the standard of living of the rural peasantry. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part II]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes 'Paibaqi' lands in the Mughal revenue administration?
opts: Lands reserved exclusively for royal gardens and hunting
Jagir lands that were yet to be allotted or were awaiting assignment
Wasted and barren lands brought under cultivation for the first time
Lands owned collectively by village artisans
practiceQuestions.sol: Paibaqi lands were those imperial lands that had not yet been assigned as jagirs to any mansabdar and remained temporarily under the administration of the central crown. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: In the Mughal agrarian economy, who was termed as 'Khud-kasht'?
opts: Migrant cultivators who leased land from village headmen on a temporary basis
Resident cultivators who owned and cultivated land in their own village
Bonded laborers who worked on the personal estates of mansabdars
Hereditary village watchmen and sweepers
practiceQuestions.sol: Khud-kasht peasants were permanent residents of the village who owned their land and ploughs, enjoying a relatively better standard of living compared to non-resident temporary cultivators (pahi-kasht). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: What role did the 'Qanungo' play in the Mughal administrative machinery?
opts: Keeper of local revenue records and customary land laws at the pargana level
Commander of the cavalry contingent stationed in urban centers
Chief judge responsible for dispensing Islamic criminal law
Superintendent of royal mints and bullion standards
practiceQuestions.sol: The Qanungo was the hereditary keeper of revenue records at the pargana (sub-district) level, maintaining data on local revenue rates, crop yields, and customary rights. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Pahi-kasht' in Mughal agrarian society refers to:
opts: Peasants who cultivated land in villages other than their own on contractual terms
Artisans engaged in silk and cotton weaving within imperial workshops (karkhanas)
Tax collectors appointed directly by the provincial diwan
Nomadic pastoralists who paid grazing taxes in livestock
practiceQuestions.sol: Pahi-kasht were non-resident cultivators who farmed lands in villages where they did not reside, often doing so because terms were more favorable or due to displacement. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, The Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following was a primary characteristic of the urban economy and elite consumption during the high Mughal period?
opts: Widespread mechanization of agricultural and textile production
High concentration of luxury manufacturing in imperial and noble 'karkhanas'
Egalitarian distribution of wealth among urban merchants and laborers
Absence of monetary exchange and reliance entirely on barter
practiceQuestions.sol: Imperial and noble karkhanas (workshops) produced luxury goods, fine textiles, weapons, and jewelry to cater to the extravagant standard of living of the Mughal ruling elite. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the structural nature of the 'Jagirdari System' directly influence the standard of living of the rural peasantry in the 17th-century Mughal Empire?
opts: Frequent transfers of Jagirdars created an incentive for them to extract maximum revenue in the short term, leading to agrarian distress.
Hereditary tenure of jagirs encouraged nobles to invest heavily in modern irrigation and crop diversification.
Jagirdars were legally prohibited from collecting revenue above fixed state rates, protecting peasants from exploitation.
The system completely eliminated intermediaries, ensuring that agricultural surplus went straight to peasant welfare.
practiceQuestions.sol: Because jagirdars were frequently transferred every few years, they had no long-term stake in the land they held, prompting them to squeeze maximum revenue from the peasantry regardless of the long-term impact on agrarian productivity and peasant living standards. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India / Irfan Habib]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the economic consequence of the influx of American silver into the Mughal Empire via global maritime trade during the 16th and 17th centuries?
opts: It caused massive deflation, making food grains extremely expensive for urban workers.
It monetized the rural economy extensively, facilitating cash revenue demands and integration into global markets.
It led to the collapse of the imperial mint system and a return to primitive barter.
It restricted trade entirely to internal land routes, isolating the Mughal economy.
practiceQuestions.sol: The influx of New World silver monetized the Mughal economy to an unprecedented degree, enabling the state to demand land revenue in cash and binding the peasantry tightly to commercial networks, though it also triggered price rises. [Primary Reference: Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-colonial India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the lifestyle and consumption patterns of the Mughal nobility (Mansabdars) impact the urban artisanal and manufacturing sectors?
opts: It depressed urban demand since nobles imported all luxury goods directly from Europe.
It stimulated urban production of luxury textiles, metalwork, carpets, and crafts, creating a thriving urban artisan class.
It forced urban artisans into bonded agricultural labor due to royal monopolies.
It had negligible impact as the nobility lived austere, self-sufficient lives.
practiceQuestions.sol: The lavish lifestyle and high consumption expenditure of the Mughal ruling elite drove demand for high-end crafts, fine muslins, silk, and intricate metalwork, sustaining a large population of urban artisans and workshops. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following best characterizes the debate among historians regarding the standard of living of the ordinary Indian peasant during the Mughal period?
opts: Unanimous agreement that peasants enjoyed high prosperity due to fertile soil and low taxes.
Polarized views between scholars pointing to abundant food grain supply versus those highlighting heavy tax burdens and subsistence crises.
General consensus that peasantry did not exist and all land was worked by state-owned slaves.
Exclusive focus on industrial workers with total neglect of agrarian conditions.
practiceQuestions.sol: While some historical interpretations emphasize that basic food grains were cheap and abundant (as noted by some European accounts), major Marxist and economic historians like Irfan Habib argue that the heavy incidence of land revenue left the average peasant living barely at subsistence level. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the intermediary class known as 'Zamindars' affect the socio-economic stratification and living standards in rural Mughal society?
opts: They acted solely as altruistic patrons who distributed their personal wealth freely among the poor.
They extracted a share of agricultural surplus (malikana) and often exercised coercive authority, contributing to rural hierarchy and exploitation.
They were completely suppressed by Akbar and played no economic role in the 17th century.
They were salaried bureaucratic officials appointed directly from Delhi with no hereditary rights.
practiceQuestions.sol: Zamindars held hereditary rights over land and a share of the produce (malikana). While some assisted in agricultural expansion, their exactions, combined with state revenue demands, heavily impacted the lower peasantry's standard of living. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the significance of cash crops (jins-i kamil) like indigo, cotton, and sugarcane in relation to the standard of living of Mughal cultivators?
opts: They were banned by the state to ensure maximum production of basic food grains.
They fetched higher market values and were encouraged by the state to meet cash revenue demands, though they required greater investment and risk.
They were exclusively cultivated in royal gardens with no participation from ordinary peasants.
They were consumed entirely by the farming households as staple diet.
practiceQuestions.sol: The cultivation of superior crops (jins-i kamil) was heavily promoted by the Mughal state because they yielded higher revenue in cash. However, they demanded higher inputs, exposing cultivators to greater market volatility and risk. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the urban-rural dichotomy manifest in terms of consumption and lifestyle during the height of the Mughal Empire?
opts: Living standards were remarkably uniform across urban and rural sectors due to decentralized village autonomy.
Urban centers concentrated massive wealth, imported luxuries, and elite consumption, whereas rural areas endured high extraction rates supporting that urban superstructure.
Rural areas were wealthier than cities because agricultural prices were artificially inflated by imperial decree.
Cities were mere administrative outposts devoid of any manufacturing or commercial consumption.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mughal urban centers functioned as drain-pipes extracting agricultural surplus from the countryside to support the luxurious consumption of the imperial court, nobility, and affluent merchants. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the socio-economic role of the village artisans (such as carpenters, blacksmiths, and weavers) within the traditional Mughal village community?
opts: They operated as independent capitalist entrepreneurs selling goods freely in international markets.
They operated within the Jajmani system, providing customary services to cultivators in exchange for a fixed share of the harvest.
They were prohibited from living inside villages and resided exclusively in fortified urban camps.
They were paid regular monthly salaries in gold coins directly from the imperial treasury.
practiceQuestions.sol: Village artisans provided essential tools, implements, and services to the peasantry under traditional customary arrangements (often linked to the jajmani system), receiving a share of the crop at harvest time rather than cash wages. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q: In what ways did the global trade integration of the Mughal Empire affect the domestic price structure and urban standard of living?
opts: It insulated the domestic market completely from foreign economic shocks through protective tariffs.
It integrated Indian textile and craft markets with global demand, boosting urban merchant wealth and artisan employment while contributing to inflationary pressures.
It destroyed all local manufacturing due to cheap European manufactured imports.
It had no bearing on prices since all foreign trade was conducted via barter without currency.
practiceQuestions.sol: Integration into global trade through European trading companies generated high demand for Indian textiles, resulting in increased monetization, commercial expansion, and urban employment, though accompanied by bullion influx and rising price trends. [Primary Reference: Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-colonial India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which factor most critically limited upward social mobility and improvement in living standards for the vast majority of the Mughal agricultural population?
opts: The rigid caste and customary stratification of rural society coupled with heavy state revenue extraction.
Absolute prohibition on owning land for anyone outside the imperial family.
A complete lack of arable land across the entire Gangetic plain.
The mandatory conversion of all peasants to military service after two generations.
practiceQuestions.sol: The combination of rigid hierarchical structures (caste/community status) and the heavy extraction of agricultural surplus by the state and intermediaries left peasants with little disposable surplus to invest or improve their social standing. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the standard of living and socio-economic conditions in Mughal India:
1. The Mughal ruling elite (Mansabdars) maintained an extraordinarily opulent lifestyle funded by the revenue extracted from the agrarian economy.
2. Foreign travellers like François Bernier noted an absence of private property in land, which he argued adversely affected the long-term investment in agricultural infrastructure.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Statement 1 reflects the extreme wealth disparity where mansabdars held massive shares of revenue. Statement 2 accurately captures Bernier's thesis that crown ownership of land discouraged long-term peasant or noble investment in land improvements compared to Europe. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part II]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about the classification of peasantry in Mughal India:
1. 'Khud-kasht' peasants were temporary migrant cultivators who leased land for a single harvest cycle.
2. 'Pahi-kasht' peasants were permanent residents of the village who owned their land and production implements.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are incorrect because their definitions are interchanged. 'Khud-kasht' were resident landowners/cultivators of the village, whereas 'Pahi-kasht' were non-resident cultivators who farmed land in villages other than their own. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Mughal Mansabdari System:
1. The mansab rank determined both the military obligations (such as horses and troopers) and the personal salary (zat and sawar) of the noble.
2. Jagirs assigned to mansabdars were hereditary estates that remained with the noble's family across generations.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; zat indicated personal status/salary and sawar indicated military contingent size. Statement 2 is incorrect because jagirs were transferable assignments, not hereditary estates; upon a mansabdar's death or transfer, the jagir reverted to the crown. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding urban conditions and artisanal production in Mughal India:
1. Imperial and noble 'karkhanas' were vital manufacturing units that produced luxury articles and specialized goods for elite consumption.
2. Urban centers in the Mughal Empire were entirely isolated from international trade networks, catering only to local hinterland needs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct as karkhanas were central to elite luxury goods production. Statement 2 is incorrect because Mughal urban centers (such as Surat, Ahmedabad, and Agra) were deeply integrated into international maritime and overland trade networks. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the taxation and agrarian revenue system under the Mughals:
1. The Zabti system instituted under Akbar involved detailed measurement of land and assessment of cash revenue rates based on historical crop yields.
2. The revenue demand was kept uniformly low across all provinces, leaving peasants with substantial savings during famine years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; the Zabti system relied on measurement (zabt) and cash schedules (dastur-al-amal). Statement 2 is incorrect because revenue demands were often heavy (taking up to a third or half of produce) and did not automatically adjust downward smoothly during local famines without immense hardship. [Primary Reference: Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the position of women in Mughal society across different strata:
1. Women belonging to the imperial household and elite families often engaged in commerce, held property rights, and received high administrative titles.
2. Women among the peasantry and working classes enjoyed equal leisure and high social standing without engaging in manual agricultural labor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; royal women like Gulbadan Begum, Nur Jahan, and Jahanara engaged in trade, patronized architecture, and held jagirs/properties. Statement 2 is incorrect because peasant women worked intensively alongside men in agricultural tasks and weaving, bearing severe economic burdens. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the agrarian economy and food consumption in Mughal India:
1. Contemporary sources indicate that basic food grains like wheat and millets were relatively cheap and abundant in normal years.
2. Famines were unknown in the Mughal Empire due to advanced state-managed grain storage and relief distribution systems.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; primary accounts note that basic grains were inexpensive. Statement 2 is incorrect because severe famines (such as the Deccan-Gujarat famine of 1630-32) periodically devastated the populace, and state relief mechanisms were rudimentary and inadequate. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding monetization and currency standards in Mughal society:
1. The Mughal silver rupee (Rupa) was renowned for its high degree of metallic purity and stability across the empire.
2. The widespread use of silver currency remained confined exclusively to royal courts, having zero impact on rural tax payments.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; the Mughal silver rupee was a standard coin of high fineness that facilitated pan-Indian commerce. Statement 2 is incorrect because monetization penetrated deep into the countryside, with peasants selling crops for cash to pay land revenue directly in coin. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the standard of living of urban wage laborers and artisans in the Mughal Empire:
1. Urban laborers and construction workers lived in extremely modest, temporary mud-and-thatch dwellings, contrasting sharply with the stone mansions of the nobility.
2. Skilled artisans working in imperial workshops received high salaries that placed them on par with mid-level Mansabdars.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; ordinary urban workers lived in poor conditions. Statement 2 is incorrect because while master artisans earned enough to survive, their economic status was far below mansabdars, and ordinary karkhana workers often faced stringent controls and modest wages. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the socio-economic impact of the Zamindari class in Mughal India:
1. Zamindars were legally entitled to a portion of the agricultural produce known as 'malikana' for performing administrative and collection duties.
2. Zamindars possessed independent armed retainers and fortresses, frequently acting as autonomous military power centers that challenged or negotiated with imperial authority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Zamindars held hereditary rights including malikana, and many powerful zamindars maintained substantial armed retainers and forts, forming an integral, often turbulent, part of the Mughal socio-political fabric. [Primary Reference: Irfan Habib, Agrarian System of Mughal India]
